prize_parts.citation: for discoveries on the incretin physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize on B033 for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange did not weaken the scientific case. It showed that all six of us rest it on the same chain: gut proglucagon peptides as the incretin, identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, receptor biology, and then decades of independent confirmation and large randomized outcome trials in glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. A discernible change in a field followed from a specific discovery, and the work is mature. I now state the citation more narrowly than in round 1. It speaks of the physiology and the identification of the active form, and it does not claim a first discovery of the incretin concept, which answers the chair's question on wording and the concern raised by Wahren-Herlenius. On the discovery-versus-development line, I would draw it at the point where the biological question is answered and the work becomes optimization of a known mechanism. By that rule Knudsen's contribution, real and decisive for the clinic, falls on the development side. The citation can acknowledge that the discoveries enabled the therapies without crediting the drug programmes.
statement.case_against: The attribution of the active peptide is still the weak point, and I cannot settle the Mojsov versus Habener question from the supplied material. Nobody in round 1 supplied primary-literature evidence that changes this, so agreement on the trio should not be read as the question being resolved. A three-person limit leaves out Knudsen and early contributors, and a physiology-only prize can be read as a judgement against translation. The cap also rules out a second distinct part, because B033 needs all three names. Long-term safety and durability in obesity are still accumulating, though I do not think that justifies deferral. If the record on the active peptide were shown to go clearly against Mojsov, I would fall back to B036 as a single-part prize rather than put an industrial name in the third slot.

responses.point: She withdrew her opening Knudsen-for-Mojsov substitution as the weaker choice, argued the citation should speak of identification of the active peptide and not a first discovery of the incretin concept, and still holds lower confidence in the exact trio than in the achievement.
responses.response: I agree with the wording and I have adopted it. The citation should name the physiology and the identification of the active form, and no more. I also share her lower confidence in the exact trio, and I do not treat her move to Mojsov as resolving it, because it rests on the same unsettled record as before. Her point that translation is an argument about wording, not about a fourth name or a swap, seems right to me. The discovery-or-development line has to be stated in the citation, or the prize will be read both ways.

responses.point: He would fall back to Drucker and Holst alone, not to an industrial name, if the committee judges the evidence on Mojsov unresolved, and he described B036 as the principal alternative for a basic-science prize.
responses.response: I take the fallback seriously, but I disagree that unresolved should lead to dropping her. Dropping a person on an unproven priority claim is itself an attribution judgement made without evidence. A pair would also be a thinner statement of a discovery that has three separable parts: the physiology, the receptor and therapeutic concept, and the active peptide. I would remove her only if the primary literature clearly showed that the identification came from others. If it did, I would prefer to move to B036 over leaving the GLP-1 prize with two names and a gap. On B036 I stay where I was: a strong science case, with the only open question being how much it matters that its disease consequences are still prospective.

responses.point: He argued that a tidy attribution on a discovery with mostly indirect clinical effect should not outrank a stronger discovery whose attribution is harder but workable within three names, and he offered to test the discovery-versus-development framing in round 2.
responses.response: I accept the test and agree with the conclusion. Cleanliness of credit is a virtue, not a substitute for effect. This is why I keep B036 as an alternative and not as the lead. I also agree that Hall alone on B043 is too narrow, and the TOR attribution is entangled as the chair says, so I no longer see B043 as a competitor this year. On discovery versus development, our positions are close. The one point I would add is that Knudsen's exclusion rests on the type of contribution and not on its size, and the committee should say so openly, so that the choice cannot be mistaken for undervaluing translation.

responses.point: He ranked B047 third and argued that a physiology-only B033 is inconsistent with B047, where drug development is the explicit achievement, and he would accept Knudsen as a fallback only after examining the priority evidence.
responses.response: The inconsistency charge is fair and I do not want to dodge it. B047 is a case where a mechanism-level discovery about splicing and the drug are one line of work by the same two people, so crediting the drug is crediting the discovery. With GLP-1 the physiological and peptide discoveries are separable from the later analogue chemistry, and academic groups made them first. That is the difference I rely on, and it is a difference of structure and not of principle. I still regard B047 as better suited to a later year, mainly for maturity and breadth of the field, as he knows from my first round. I would keep Knudsen out even in his fallback case unless the committee first decides to reward translation.

responses.point: He asked the committee to examine the primary publications and Habener's role before moving off Mojsov, argued that the evidence does not support waiting on safety data, and as chair listed B013 with Rosenberg as a defensible alternative.
responses.response: I agree on the order of work: examine the record first, then decide the name. I also agree that safety and durability do not justify waiting, because the mechanism and the outcome trials are already settled and later data would refine the drug class and not the discovery. On B013 I have come to his side and to Wahren-Herlenius's: June and Sadelain are the cleaner pair, and Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is an earlier, separate line, so I would now list B013 as a second alternative in place of B011. I note again that he and I have co-authored, which I flagged in round 1, and it did not affect my weighting.

uncertainties: Whether the primary literature supports crediting Mojsov for the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide against the claims of Habener and colleagues. I cannot resolve this from the supplied evidence.
Whether the discovery-versus-development line I draw, which excludes Knudsen, will be accepted as principled and not as undervaluing translation.
Whether mammalian PERK and ATF6 contributors on B036 and Eshhar on B013 are omissions that would change the fallback ranking.
Long-term safety and durability of GLP-1 agents in obesity, which I do not regard as a reason to defer.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. No conflict is apparent with any credited name on the shortlist. My research on nuclear receptors and dopamine neurons does not overlap the GLP-1 candidates, and my past co-authorship with Ronald Evans and collaboration with Johan Ericson do not involve any shortlisted candidate. I disclose co-authored work with Per Svenningsson, the chair, and one paper with Abdel El Manira. Neither is a candidate, and I do not regard either as grounds for recusal.
